question_text:
Premise 1: All department heads are career service eligible.
Premise 2: Maria is a department head.
Which conclusion logically follows?

options.text: Maria is not career service eligible.
All career service eligibles are department heads.
Maria will be promoted next year.

hint_ladder.title: Picture the Sets
hint_ladder.text: Think of two circles: a small one labeled 'department heads' and a big one labeled 'career service eligible.' Premise 1 tells you the small circle fits completely inside the big one. Now, where does Maria go?

hint_ladder.title: Place Maria in the Picture
hint_ladder.text: Premise 2 says Maria is a department head, so put her inside the small circle. Since the small circle is entirely inside the big circle, what does that mean for Maria?

hint_ladder.title: Follow the Chain
hint_ladder.text: If everything in the small circle is also in the big circle, and Maria is in the small circle, then she must be in the big circle too. This is a simple logical chain: All A are B, Maria is A, so Maria is B.

hint_ladder.title: Spot the Right Match
hint_ladder.text: Option B says exactly that: Maria is career service eligible. Option A says the opposite, which would break the chain. Option C flips the relationship around, and Option D brings in something new that wasn't mentioned at all.

A.text: This directly contradicts the premises. If all department heads are eligible and Maria is a department head, she can't be ineligible. It's like saying 'all birds can fly' and then claiming a sparrow can't fly.

B.text: Correct. This is a clean logical deduction: if everything in group A belongs to group B, and Maria is in group A, then Maria belongs to group B. Simple and airtight.

C.text: This is a common trap called the converse fallacy. Just because all department heads are eligible doesn't mean all eligible people are department heads. Think of it like 'all dogs are mammals' — that doesn't mean all mammals are dogs.

D.text: This introduces a new idea (promotion) that wasn't in the premises at all. Logical conclusions can only use the information given, not add assumptions about the future.

next_time_rule: When you see 'All A are B,' picture a small circle inside a big circle. If something is in the small circle, it's automatically in the big circle. Never flip it around — that's a classic trap.
deconstruct_text: Let's walk through this step by step. The first premise gives you a rule: all department heads are career service eligible. Think of it as a membership rule — if you're in the 'department head' club, you're automatically in the 'career service eligible' club. The second premise tells you Maria is a department head. So she's in that first club, which means she's also in the second club. That's why option B is correct. Option A would mean she's not in the second club, which breaks the rule. Option C tries to reverse the rule, but that's not what the premises say. Option D brings in promotions, which is a whole new topic not mentioned anywhere. The key mental trick here is the 'circle test': draw a small circle inside a big one. If you're in the small one, you're in the big one. That's all you need.
